documents.title: Why Art?
paragraphs: Creativity is the creation of an Other: a text, an object, an event. Perception is the experience of encountering the Other, of comprehending it through oneself, of discovering it within oneself. Discovering the Other within oneself requires assimilating it, accepting or rejecting it. To accept the Other means becoming other oneself — becoming larger by the measure of the Other. The fear of accepting the Other is the fear of changing and no longer being what one was. The fear of discovering the Other within oneself, or oneself as other, is the fear of discovering oneself, one's expansive, expanding essence.

An encounter with the Other is almost always stressful. Art prepares a person for an encounter with the Other. The territory of art is a safe training ground for the soul. Art knocks a person out of the comfort zone, leads them out of a recognizable, stable landscape. Art develops — and causes development — where shoots of the new, the other, break through the asphalt of an assimilated, established tradition. Mozart is a genius not where he submits to genre but where he overcomes its dictate. Those who change the world are those open to changing themselves, to acknowledging another point of view, taste, gesture.

New art places a question mark after every statement; it subjects it to doubt. A person, by contrast, more often seeks confirmation of the self in the repetition of experience — repetition and confirmation sustain the illusion of stability. Karl Marx proposes that a person become aware of themselves through a permanent inner revolution. But beyond liberation, what awaits a person except themselves, stripped of the familiar shell of stereotypes and inevitably acquiring a new one?

If one does not open the door to the Other, one can preserve the hope that there is an Other behind it — the hope of not being alone. The Other is an enemy: it has come to make me other, to become another me. Fear of the Other turns out to be fear of loneliness, fear of oneself. The path of knowing oneself through accepting the Other is a path of multiplying loneliness, a path toward becoming aware of oneself as a multiplicity, a community: I-multiplicity, I-community.

But if there is only I, I-multiplicity, then is all the vileness I encounter in life and flee from also me? In what situation do I make the inner choice to be vile? When I do not allow the Other to be other, when I seek to subordinate or eliminate them, to impose my will upon them — when I do not allow myself to become other. I am vile to the extent that I allow myself to think of the Other as vile. Every evaluative construction is self-referential.

documents.title: I-Community
paragraphs: The signs we decide to write down, the sounds or actions we decide to produce or perform, do not ask us to be written, produced, or performed — they appear by our will, by our authoritarian decision. Likewise, children do not ask us to be born into this world. This decision is an act of life-giving violence. Life on earth is sustained by a chain of acts of life-giving violence. In committing such an act, we accept responsibility for the child born, the sign written, the sound produced. What is a repeated act of violence in relation to the first child, sign, sound? From a situation of attention to the uniqueness of a singular phenomenon we enter a situation of multiplicity, a situation that demands relationships between phenomena — relationships structured hierarchically or in some other way.

For a long time, the history of music dealt with relationships between sounds. Sounds were subordinated to a center or arranged within various fixed modal or serial structures. Music — the European professional tradition — moved from constructing relationships between sounds toward ever greater attention to a single sound as a complete phenomenon. Eventually a single sound could generate complex systems, as in spectralism; a single sound became a self-sufficient individual world.

Musical genres similarly moved from the anonymous universality of liturgical service toward the personification of style, when a particular genre, style, or tradition becomes associated with a specific composer or even with a single work in which that style or genre is exhausted. Humanity likewise moves from collective means of survival, organization of labor, and methods of warfare toward individual ones; from centrist and hierarchical social systems toward the search for systems guaranteeing independence and equality.

With the course of history, we can observe humanity moving from the idea of the collective and multiple toward the idea of the individual and singular. We see the value of the individual world of a single person becoming absolute — and in art, the value of a single sound, a single sign.

It is interesting that every regression in social organization entails a regression in other forms of activity: dictatorships of the twentieth — and now the twenty-first — century have used as an ideological weapon art in which the significance of the center is emphasized to the maximum, proclaiming hierarchy.

Every person feels in their own way; every person must recognize and learn to value the dissimilarity of the Other. Difference and respect for difference are a condition of human survival today. Art helps to emphasize this difference, to accept and respect it. Responsibility toward the singular phenomenon is one of the key concepts defining the field of art and human relations today. It seems that the function of art today is to separate. By exposing difference, art makes it possible to see the whole in the part and thus discover a multiplicity of wholes. If previously the part was smaller than the whole, in postmodernism the part equals the whole; post-postmodernism makes the part larger than the whole.

Every attempt at unification today becomes a cause of discord, war, and misunderstanding. The idea of unification transfers personal responsibility to a phantom majority — or, more precisely, to a particular person or group assuming the function of expressing a collective will. Today we all live in separate autonomous worlds, within geographical and political borders different from those drawn on physical or political maps. My country has borders different from the borders of the country in which I formally reside. One person, one sign, one sound contain within themselves a unique multiplicity, community, totality, completeness. Semantic units are born such as I-community, sign-multiplicity, sound-consonance.

documents.title: Author vs Avatar
paragraphs: When an artist deals with convention, with ready-made, historically conditioned models of writing, the question of authorship arises: does the artist write the model, or does the model write the artist? Having no other means, the model uses the artist for self-reproduction; the artist becomes the model's instrument, its avatar. This does not negate artistic mastery — mastery in handling the model. But even a skillful overcoming of the model, however free an interpretation, however much the individual is made to grow through the collective, does not cancel the primary conditioning by the model.

Individuality, dissimilarity, is given to every person from birth — there is no second me. In searching for the new, the Other, one need not look far: it can be discovered within oneself. But this otherness makes a person lonely. This is why we are oriented toward the search for unity, a unifying idea, common ideals. When we see two identical objects, we make no effort to discover their differences. When we see two different objects, we search for similarities and try to classify them.

In music, the collective presupposes foundations — genres, styles, techniques — accepted by large communities over long periods. The individual, by contrast, can be compared with the personification of styles and genres, when an individual person, an author, becomes a style and a genre. Today every author is potentially a style, a genre, an epoch. A single work can become an epoch: John Cage's 4'33" is a historical epoch lasting four minutes and thirty-three seconds.

It seems that the present situation is characterized by the emancipation of the author from the non-authorial, of the individual from the collective. Vladimir Martynov's concept of the end of the time of composers is, in my view, a statement of the death of the collective author, but it ignores the birth of the individual author.

Previously there was a system of genres: everyone wrote minuets or sonatas. These are non-personified phenomena. Whether Mozart exists or not, the minuet and sonata existed and will continue to exist. But when we hear, for example, György Ligeti's music, we hear precisely Ligeti — an absolutely personified style enclosed within one author. The Classical era, like the Baroque or Romantic era, is an epoch of the collective author, existing for decades in many bodies. Their bodies became avatars of this collective author. Mozart is a genius not where he submits to genre but where he overcomes it.

The collective gives rise to the formula: what belongs to everyone belongs to no one. It seems that one can play with the models of collective epochs, appropriate them, and claim with some justification the right to do so. Postmodern culture was precisely such a transpersonal game. With the birth of a new personality, a new wholeness, with the personification of an epoch, the postmodern paradigm dissolved. Ligeti is an individual, personified style. Appropriating Ligeti enters the territory of plagiarism and copyright.

When I sit down before a blank sheet, I do not see it as blank; on the contrary, it is black with writing — all existing and non-existing music has been inscribed upon it in many layers. Music already written, music that will still be written, and music that will never be written. Composition is not the placing of signs on paper but the clearing away of what is unnecessary, as an archaeologist clears layers of sand and dust. In other words, creativity is refusal — and the more we refuse, the more unique our choice becomes. Ultimately, in making a choice, we choose, we discover ourselves.
Creativity is when, amid all the diversity of choice, we stop at what does not exist.

In a situation of total personification, of the emancipation of style, genre, a single sound or silence, the illusion of permissiveness arises: everything is possible. Perhaps it is. But this 'everything is possible' is not an external choice made by a postmodern author-operator imagining themselves outside the system. It is the system itself, the sum of differences coexisting in a single moment of historical time, the sum of everything possible. Each difference is a unique personified unit that must be distinguished. Having finished playing the outsider, however interested, the author has entered the system, become it, and is occupied with choosing themselves.

At the next stage, this 'everything is possible' encounters the performer, spectator, listener, who in turn make their own choice and ultimately discover themselves as well. This choice is an equally significant creative act. Thus the listener becomes a creator, and perception becomes a new institution of creativity.

documents.title: The Art of Perception
paragraphs: I do not really believe in the listener, the spectator — in their existence. There are only my constructs, my ideas of the spectator, that is, myself. Conventionally speaking, the artist composes not only the text but also the spectator. The question is whether the spectator wants to be composed, since they may feel a certain aggression directed at them in this act: the artist wants to make them other. Is a person ready to change? That belongs to the territory of individual motivations, situations, and biographies.

But the spectator and listener, in turn, compose what they see and hear. The newer, the more 'incomprehensible' the object of perception, the greater the creative demand placed on the listener's perception. With classical examples it seems easier: there are conventions, assimilated models of perception. But this is an apparent simplicity — often we find ourselves dealing not with the object of perception itself but with conventions of perception, behind which the object itself may disappear.

Who am I? Who are you? Where are we? At every moment we ask ourselves these questions anew and construct the answers, these 'where' and 'who'. Such construction is the art of perception: perception as another institution of creativity alongside music, literature, visual art, choreography. Perception — in the particular case of music, listening — is not the reception of information but construction. The construction of what lies behind sound, behind the surface of sound. Sounds are surfaces that lead us away, distract us from what matters. Listening to sounds is like looking at a pane of glass without noticing what lies behind it. The fetishization of sounds leaves us on the surface, judging only its irregularities.

I am trying to consider 'hearing' in the context of a radical departure beyond the audible. Continuing the metaphor of glass: sound is a door, an obstacle that must be overcome in order to see the landscape hidden behind it.

Chinese painting has the concept of liu bai — omission, intentional blankness: the artist leaves parts of the canvas unpainted, allowing us only to guess what might be depicted there. Perception is the art of experiencing what is not on the surface. The art of hearing beyond sounds, beyond words, of seeing beyond images. Contemporary art is often about this: first in overcoming illustration, and then in overcoming form itself.

Perception is a creative act: listening, we create what we hear; reading, we create what we read; observing, we create what we see. Perception is a mechanism available to everyone for translating everyday reality into artistic reality. It requires no socially restrictive superstructures or filters — concert halls, theaters, ticket offices, schedules. Perception has no externally imposed format, whether historical tradition or aesthetic school; its format is personified — it is the perceiver, their biography and psychophysics. In perception we learn ourselves — from ourselves.

Why do I write? To transmit knowledge? But if I myself am certain of nothing, then I can only share my uncertainty, transmit not-knowing. I do not know. And where I think I know, I am mistaken. Everyone knows in the same way, but does not know — guesses — differently. Just as sounds prevent us from hearing and images from seeing, by transmitting knowledge might I not close off the possibility of acquiring it?

Do we need sounds in order to hear, words in order to understand? The art of perception lies beyond the surface of sound or word. We can perceive a visual situation aurally and vice versa. All we need is a voluntary decision, an agreement, a consent to perceive something in a particular way.

Unexpectedly, on the territory of pure perception, the role of trust grows: mutual trust, respect, agreement. What we so often lack turns out to exist in abundance on the territory where the arts are not divided according to formal attributes, where in principle nothing is divided according to formal attributes and, consequently, no attributes need to be defended against others.
Having lost their forms-surfaces, all arts meet on the common territory of perception, the territory of trust. A territory on which the artwork itself becomes a kind of figure of omission. Liu bai.
